title: Planning renewable energy in rural areas: Impacts on occupation and land use
abstract: Reflecting on the role of rural areas in the 21st century is, nowadays, a central theme in the important debate on the long-term renewable energy development. It is the case that while cities demonstrate an ever-growing pattern of energy consumption, rural areas keep themselves as almost low-density territories and with the greatest potential of renewable energy sources. This means a new smart specialization of rural areas as green energy exporters to fuel urban areas, providing effective and long-lasting answers to the climate change, the reduction of energy dependency and respective social, economic and environmental impacts. Nevertheless, the implementation of renewable energy sources requires safeguarding the balance between occupation and land use and, at the same time, preservation and respect for the environmental, cultural and scenic values of these privileged territories. The present paper describes the first stage of an exploratory empirical study on the various impacts caused by the implementation of different renewable energy sources in rural areas. With reference to the County of Loures in Portugal, factors and geographical determinants, underlying the localization of recently implemented photovoltaic power plants and wind farms, have been identified. The level 5 Corine Land Cover 2007 datasets and satellite images have been used along with the information collected during on-site field work. The delimitation of infrastructure areas associated with renewable energy production, has enabled an understanding of the changes in land occupation over the time period of a decade and how these aspects are linked to the spatial dimensions of planning and land management. The results obtained demonstrate the emergence of a functional dichotomy between the preservation of lands with strong agricultural potential and the massive expansion of renewable energy production across rural areas. This allows us to understand how the implementation of renewable energy sources is ever more linked to the local decision-making process associated with spatial planning. The role that municipalities can play in the definition of strategies to ensure an efficient, balanced and sustainable renewable energy zoning in rural areas will therefore be crucial.

## 1. Introduction

At present, rural areas occupy 90% of European Union territory and contain 57.4% of its population [1], playing a determinant role in sustainable development. In this context, the need for tackling climate change and CO2 emissions provides ever increasing challenges, namely the possibilities to explore endogenous energy potential [2]. It is the case that while cities demonstrate an ever-

(A. Firmino), miguelpamado@tecnico.ulisboa.pt (M. Amado).

growing pattern of energy consumption, rural areas keep themselves as almost low-density territories, with the greatest potential of renewable energy sources.

Within the urgent challenge to reinvent, rethink and rebuild territories according to a process of adaptation to energy descent [3], it is thus essential to understand the key role that rural areas can actually play, paving the way forward for this transition. Indeed, the organizational model of rural areas that has always been based on the three pillars: 1. production of food e main function, 2. agriculture e main economic activity, 3. balance between natural features and human activities carried out e form of landscape, is inevitably changing [4]. In this context, the implementation of renewable energy sources is a new aspect of development which

may improve and enhance the competitiveness, smart specialization and economic growth of rural areas [5].

However, sustainability is the keyword underlying every development process [6], a principle which, when analyzed from the perspective of renewable energy sources in rural areas, should be accompanied by another, equally imperative concept which is to preserve the land and safeguard the natural and cultural landscape [7]. In a future scenario where fossil fuels will no longer be able to ensure the global energy supply [8], there will have to be a sustainable renewable energy sources mix embedded within rural areas [9]. Here, a critical challenge is planning for a comprehensive model which involves urban and rural areas as an energetically balanced whole [10]. Indeed, this assumption aims to simplify the relationships between the complex and uncertain dynamics regarding energy transition and policy decision-making [11]. In this framework, the present study aims to investigate the fundamental trade-off between the preservation of rural areas and the need of using parts of them for renewable energy production.

The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents a state-ofthe-art review of the relationships between renewable energy and rural areas; Section 3 describes the methodology to asses renewable energy sources impacts in rural areas; Section 4 illustrates the practical application of the methodology in a case study; Section 5 discusses the results, articulating the potential optimization of a renewable energy mix and the land utilization, from local planning perspective; Section 6 draws out the key conclusions.

## 2. Renewable energy and rural areas

Substituting fossil fuels with renewable energy sources is a process of utmost importance to fight climate change [12] and contribute to world primary energy needs [13]. In the last decade, the contribution of renewable energy sources to the current EU-28 energy mix has seen high growth rates (Fig. 1). In particular, wind and solar energy are experiencing a substantial expansion due to the strong cost reductions and fewer sustainability concerns than the other low-carbon power supply options [14].

Meanwhile, current energy planning scenario has multiple objectives, definitions and criteria making it more difficult to attain a system with a perception of sustainability [16]. The latter aspect is directly related to the technological, functional and geographical specificity of each resource and the effective hierarchy in terms of decision-making and spatial planning at national, regional, intermunicipal and municipal levels. Studies that have specifically focused on the role of global planning level and renewable energy source implementation substantially confirmed the below table (Table 1) [17e23].

The analysis carried out on the main renewable energy resources and the respective global level of planning enables to conclude that municipalities, through diagnosing and defining the development assumptions inherent to each renewable energy source, can play a key role in sustainable energy planning at the local level [18], [21] and [22].

Fig. 1. Electricity produced from renewable sources in the EU-28 [15].

In this context, it is important to underline that if the main patterns of energy demand and CO2 emissions occur in the cities, the main supply of renewable energy sources is to be found in the countryside [24]: this is a privileged space in the territory for the production of clean energy. A strategy that targets renewable energy flows requires a decentralized planning perspective, in order to manage the relatively low power densities and intermittency associated with these resources [25]. A critical point here is that renewable energy sources imply intensive land use [26].

It should therefore be noted that the issue of the use and occupancy of land and its relationship with the spatial dimension of renewable sources is an essential sustainability criteria for the correct implementation of these technologies [27]. Indeed, the implementation of renewable energy sources in the countryside, irrespective of their nature and size, involves dealing with particularly sensitive linked issues such as land occupancy for food production [28], as well as the conservation of nature and the preservation of landscapes [29]. In this regard, the focus of the present paper is the analytical framework regarding solar and wind energy implementation at the municipal level, and their specific impacts on land use in rural areas.

The use of solar energy is one of the most promising energy alternatives to meet the challenge of a sustainable future in environmental terms [17]. However, it is always necessary to take into consideration that solar radiation levels are variable during the day, depend on the period of the year and are influenced by atmospheric phenomena, and are also obviously zero during night-time [13]. These aspects mean that solar energy cannot be considered a single solution, but only a contribution within the renewable energy mix that ensures the supply of electricity to territories. The implementation of this type of resource, associated with microgeneration technologies (photovoltaic panels and solar collectors) on the roofs of buildings is an opportunity with great potential to ensure more energy efficient buildings [30]. Nevertheless, it is the introduction of photovoltaic power plants for the production of electricity on a large scale that would have more significant impacts on the countryside and its natural values and cultural heritage [31]. The implementation of this technology can lead to the complete loss of land and agricultural activity, and this is a rather important consequence with regard to its local development [32]. Moreover, the utilization of rural areas for solar energy production can result in social equity impacts associated with the land values that are lowest and with the existing users which often have less power and fewer formal land rights [33].

On the other hand, wind power, from the earliest days to its discovery and usage through windmills has been a resource generating development in the rural world. In recent years, wind power has affirmed itself as a more economically and technically viable and renewable source [34]. It should be added that wind power does not create waste or emit pollutants, and therefore is a valuable contribution towards greenhouse gas reduction [35]. Wind power has a significant annual variability, with higher production during the winter [36]. In spatial terms, wind-generated electricity is implemented in the form of wind farms: sets of wind turbines connected to an electricity substation [34]. The implementation of this technology is limited by the availability of places with sufficient wind (at least 20 km per hour) and the number of production units that a certain area can accommodate [37]. In this context it is important to mention that the turbines occupy only 2% of the area, with most of the surrounding soil being used for the production of vegetables, nurseries and feeding cattle [37]. On the other hand, the “wind farms-rural areas” relationship leads to the controversial debate about the various environmental impacts and which involve issues related to the landscape [38], noise [39], bird deaths due to collisions [40] and the widespread

## 3. Methodology

This article presents the first stage of an exploratory empirical study on the various impacts caused by the implementation of renewable energy sources in rural areas. As such, the methodology has been structured into three stages (Fig. 2):

- 1) delimitation of the areas occupied by renewable energy production infrastructures, developed through the visual interpretation of satellite images provided by Google Earth along with the information collected during on-site field work. It should be noted that two types of spatial cells for renewable energy production have been defined: the linear cell for central wind farms and the compact cell for photovoltaic farms;

- 2) analysis of the evolution of land use and occupation in a time scale of a decade;

- 3) overlap of different cells delimited in the level 5 Corine Land Cover 2007 (CLC2007) land occupancy/use map.

In this context, it is to refer that all the domains associated with renewable energy planning are geographical information-based. Palmas, Siewert, & Von Haaren (2015) advocate that it is necessary to combine spatial information on both, sectorial and combined renewable energy potentials as well as possible environmental impacts. In turn, these authors demonstrate that

different information layers can be integrated by Geographical Information System (GIS) for assessing spatial implications and land requirements of each renewable energy technology and possible energy mix.

In order to deal with the uncertainty of input parameters that characterizes strategic energy planning [42], the proposed methodology undertakes an empirical approach to rural areas where renewable energy sources have been already implemented. This permits to reduce epistemic uncertainties by gathering data through direct observation i.e. CLC2007, reliable statistics, analysis of satellite images in GIS environment and field work. The result is an approach that differs from the literature that focus on the assessment of the renewable energy-mix and land use, exploring the potential impacts in the future and not the real ones [42] [43].

## 4. Case study: the County of Loures

The methodology described above was applied to the County of Loures in Portugal. The case study is integrated in the region of Lisbon and Tagus Valley - NUTII of Greater Lisbon, being part of the Metropolitan Area of Lisbon (Fig. 3).

With an area of about 1672 Km[2] and a population of 208,858 inhabitants, Loures is a county marked by its rural character, with the area of farms representing more than 50% of the territory (Fig. 4). Indeed, the population distribution is quite uneven in the territory, since the Southern part, next to Lisbon is most densely populated, followed by an intermediate area and the Northern part is less populated and presents a more rural character.

The promotion of renewable energy has proven to be one of the greatest challenges the Loures county faced over the last years. Loures signed the Covenant of Mayors in 2010, with the aim to enforce sustainability principles at the municipal level [44]. The Sustainable Energy Action Plans of Loures demonstrates the active involvement of the local government in attracting stakeholders for renewable energy projects by means of administrative simplification of licensing procedures [44]. Moreover, Loures is one of the 43 municipalities involved in the RENER Living Lab which, operating as a Smart Cities Network in Portugal, aims at i) generating information and knowledge to support policy-making processes; ii) promoting initiatives focused in one or more of the smart city areas: governance, energy, mobility, quality of life, etc.

In this context, it is important to mention the significant exploitation of renewable energy sources, in particular wind and solar energy, existing in Loures that results from the geo-climatic and physiographic conditions inherent to the territory. The municipal energy system is now complemented by three photovoltaic installations: Olival da Quinta Nova, Sao[~] Juliao[~] do Tojal, the MARL e Supply Market of the Lisbon Area and five wind farms of varying sizes (Fig. 5).

In terms of electricity production, the County of Loures has made a significant contribution, accounting for about 50.77% of the total energy produced by wind and solar resources at the national

From the analysis of data relating to solar radiation it is possible to verify that the Loures county presents excellent conditions for exploiting microgeneration, minigeneration and solar thermal technologies and implementing large scale photovoltaic power plants to provide for urban population agglomerates.

On the other hand, the state of maturity of wind power technology makes the production of electricity of great quality profitable through sets of aerogenerators installed in wind farms, while allowing the continuation of activities (e.g. agricultural activities) in the surrounding terrain [13].

The visual interpretation of satellite images provided by Google Earth along with the information collected during on-site field work enabled the localization and delimitation of the solar energy and wind power production units installed in the county. In terms of solar energy, three photovoltaic power plants were identified (Table 2).

The delimitation of infrastructure areas necessary for renewable energy production, enables an understanding of the type of changes in land occupation over the time and how these aspects are linked to the spatial dimensions of planning and land management.

In this way, Fig. 10 shows the development of land occupancy and use in the areas where the photovoltaic power plants are currently located, from 2002 until 2016.

Through this analysis it is possible to see how the implementation of the two ground-mounted solar power plants at S[~] ao Juliao do Tojal and Olival da Quinta Nova led to profound changes in[~] the land occupation/use. The loss of territorial dynamics and

diversity is evident when comparing the “before and after” photos of the installation of the photovoltaic plants. In the case of Sao[~] Juli[~] ao do Tojal plant, it should be mentioned that thousands of pine trees and other species from the Paradise Forest were felled during its construction. The construction of Olival da Quinta Nova plant caused the complete destruction of an orchid-rich area.

On the other hand, the MARL plant, encouraging the installation of photovoltaic panels in the large roofing of the supply market buildings and slopes of the surrounding area, has enabled electricity production with minimal environmental and landscaping impact.

Also with regard to issues related to land occupancy, the overlap of the renewable energy production cells delimited with the CLC2007 has allowed a more rigorous assessment of the alterations in the percentage of uses regarding the areas occupied by each photovoltaic installation (Table 3). As for the land use analysis due to the installation of wind farms, the decision to provide a sample was taken. Out of the 30 wind turbines currently installed in the territory of Loures, grouped into five wind farms (Fig. 5), the two with the largest sizes have been selected: Fanhoes[~] and Fontelas farms, both with 9 wind turbines generating 18 MW of power (Fig. 11).

The cells which result from the delimitation of the wind farms are of a linear type. The criteria underlying this delimitation was to consider a buffer of 200 m from the line connecting the different wind turbines in order to take into account the size of their blades (about 80 m in diameter) and the surrounding area, roads and appended infrastructure. In this regard, Table 4 summarises the overlap of wind energy production cells with CLC2007.

Analysis of overlap with CLC2007 has shown that the wind farms take up a much greater land occupation than the photovoltaic installations. However, the land uses in the area covered by the wind farms installation did not undergo important changes, as it was still possible to keep the existing activities and natural resources.

## 5. Results and discussion

The study carried out discusses the potential contributions that renewable energy sources can bring to the process of sustainable energy development for society. In particular, it tackles the problems and opportunities involved in the process of producing clean energy and the respective repercussions on occupation and land use in rural areas. The results obtained have shown the emergence of a new functional dichotomy between the preservation of agricultural land and the expansion of renewable energy production in rural areas. Producing an extremely detailed analysis through the perspective of spatial planning is a fundamental step to plan renewable energy in rural areas and prevent impacts on occupation and land use. In this sense, the undertaking of this case study has shown some of the main impacts that photovoltaic power plants and wind farms can have on these areas.

As indicated, ground-mounted solar power plants present a type of dense physical land occupation (Fig. 12-a) and should only be permitted in areas which are not farmable and with no natural scenic value. Wind farms, characterized by a more occasional occupation (Fig. 12-b), ensure minimal impact on the use/occupancy of the land, it is however necessary to mitigate certain cognitive and psychological barriers linked to the development of this resource. The correct implementation of renewable energy sources such as solar energy and wind power, which are planned at the local level, constitutes a key aspect in ensuring that decision-making is undertaken within the principles of sustainable rural areas planning. But, renewable energy sources do not only involve the problem of their allocation and the preservation of agricultural features and natural and cultural values. They are part of a comprehensive model that has to be associated with matching energy supply and demand at global scale. Here, the role that municipalities can play in the definition of specific strategies in order to ensure an efficient, balanced and sustainable renewable energy zoning in rural areas will therefore be crucial. As such, it is to conclude that, while the opportunity to promote renewable energy resources is recognized, it must be the case that a sustainable energy planning process is defined for rural areas, to enable this to be operationalized in an integrated manner with considerations firmly based on the municipal context. This process should be accompanied by the current regime for land use planning, so that the issue of renewable energies is regulated specifically by territorial management instruments.

The first environmental concern deals with the definition of spatial strategies that ensure a sustainable energy planning for rural areas, where ecological sensitivity, agriculture, wetlands, forestland and cultural components are clearly delimited and protected. The second technical aspect leads to a foreseeable scenario where energy balance between renewable energy producers and end-users is implemented by means of smart grid.

A number of critic consequences and fundamental opportunities thus emerges and from them, it is to refer that the implementation of renewable energy sources in rural areas has to revolve around small-scale interventions integrated in municipal planning. In this way, the combination of information such as satellite images, onsite field work and CLC2007 data in a GIS, permits to extend the methodology applied to the case of Loures, over each municipality or other local contexts which can be involved within the energy transition process.

## 6. Conclusions

Discussion around the model of energy production stemming from renewable sources shows the need to control the implementation process of these technologies so as to avoid conflicts with land use/occupancy in rural areas. As such, exploiting renewable energy sources clearly provides a new form of competition for land, which brings pressure to all territories, resulting from the need for urbanization and at the same time the preservation of forest areas, natural resources and lands with recognized agricultural features. The implementation of renewable energy sources thus requires the formulation of a new rural land zoning which is compatible with protecting the landscape, preserving biodiversity and, in turn, which can be coherently integrated within municipal planning and management.
